doc.title: Jason Palmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2025

chapter: Sideman career and finding a sound
title: Transcribing trumpeters, finding his voice and sideman versatility
summary: Palmer describes transcribing Nicholas Payton, Clifford Brown and others, John McNeil at NEC, and building a sound from many trumpeters.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Sidney Bechet: the man, the horn, the legend

blocks.x: I’ve read your list of albums under your own name, and then I guess about 40 albums as a sideman.
Yeah I’m up to about a hundred now.
Now you’re up to a hundred.
Yeah, it’s not up to date, yeah.
Well that helps me with my question. Why? Why do so many other jazz musicians want you on their recordings? So set your modesty aside and tell me.

Oh Jeez I wish I knew. Well you know the trumpet is a very — I wouldn’t want to say unforgiving but it’s an instrument that takes a lot of work to really make it a very malleable instrument. It’s an instrument that, it takes a lot, you’ve got to do a lot of work on yourself. I mean you have to, it’s kind of like being, I don’t know, like an opera singer. You know you have to have proper breath control, embouchure support and you know it’s unlike most all other wind instruments. Maybe French horn is maybe just as challenging of an instrument to perform on, but I think for me you know I put a lot of work into, Jeez, that’s a tough question. But you know what? What I did in college is I did a whole bunch of transcribing. I transcribed as many different trumpet players as a could. When I got to New England Conservatory back in 1997 I probably knew five trumpet players off the top of my head. I knew Clifford Brown’s playing, I had transcribed some of him; Miles Davis; I was familiar with Dizzy; Louis Armstrong; and Freddie Hubbard; and Nicholas Payton. My trumpet player in high school introduced me to the music of Nicholas Payton. We listened to “Gumbo Nouveau” and “Whoopin’ Blues” was one of my first transcriptions. I transcribed him. And so when I got to NEC my teacher, bless his soul — he passed away back in September, John McNeil, told me about all these other trumpet players I needed to listen to. So what I ended up doing is, you know, going out and finding records and recordings and going to the library and listening to LPs of all the players that influenced the players that I had already listened to, you know Fats Navarro, you know Roy Eldridge, you know Chet Baker, Woody Shaw, Lee Morgan you know just so many other you know great players. And I started transcribing, learning as much as I could just taking in things, going to concerts and you know sneaking into Wally’s you know I was underage at the time. So I did a lot of transcribing and just absorbing different styles in the hopes of trying to get to a point where I had like a visualization of like going into a room of like a whole bunch of trumpet players and saying okay Miles is over here, Fats is over here, bla-bla-bla, bla-bla- bla. This is the whole trumpet creative space. Where’s the empty space where I can find where I can just lay, you know, all of the stuff that I’m playing and just be there and have it be a thing where it’s identifiable but it’s still influenced by everybody else in the room. So I tried to absorb as many different styles as possible in order to try to find who I truly am as a creative person you know so when someone listens to me they’ll say, “Okay that’s Jason because there’s a little bit of Booker Little, there’s a little bit of Freddie,

there’s a little bit of who — but it’s all — it’s none of those people it’s just like a combination of all those people. And so you know I want to say that people that hire me might hear that in my playing, but you know that’s kind of not a question for me I guess. On the other side of it I really enjoy like playing in other people’s bands and helping them bring their music to life. You know I end up getting called to play in bands with people who write really complicated music that’s beautiful at the same time. So I don’t know that could be a thing. I don’t know there’s a handful of us that are in that realm. You know when I listen to other trumpet players who have influenced me and my generation like that I think of people like Ambrose Akinmusire, Jonathan Finlayson, Sean Jones, Philip Dizak, Adam O’Farrill, you know those trumpet players they have that thing where they have a very unique, recognizable voice and they also have this musicality that allows them to be almost chameleon-like where they can fit into a lot of different situations, which is something that we kind of have to have nowadays because you know very few people I know play in just one band and they just do that. You know, unless you’re a leader and you’ve got a lot of support. But you know as a trumpet player you know I’ve made a hefty amount of my career has been playing as a sideperson in other people’s bands. You know I’m doing my first tour as a leader overseas in October of this year. And I’m 46 years old and I’ve never taken a band out under my own name. So all the traveling that I’ve done has been in other people’s bands up until now.
